messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi Patel is a 68-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment months after being raped in a building where he had been staying overnight for work with the nonprofit that employs him. He has found it almost impossible to describe the assault directly. In the first sessions he circled around it, saying he knew exactly what happened but could not find words for it, as if language stopped where the worst part began. What comes back most clearly are sounds and sensations: a footstep in the hallway, the shift of a door, the attacker’s breathing, and the pain in his body in the same places that were hurt that night. Those fragments make ordinary noises feel charged. Even now, if he hears an unexpected sound in his apartment or in the office after hours, his body reacts as though someone may be entering.

In the weeks afterward, Ravi had come to believe that the way he was reacting meant something shameful about him. He was certain that a stronger man would have coped better, spoken more clearly, and moved on. He told himself that since the assault he was a lousy coper, permanently changed, cut off from the ordinary emotional life other people seemed to have. As a divorced older man who already felt somewhat separate from younger coworkers, he began to experience himself as an outsider in a more final way, as though the assault had pushed him beyond the edge of ordinary human belonging. These conclusions did not stay abstract. The more he judged himself as broken and permanently different, the more he watched for danger, listening for signs of intrusion at home and remaining on high alert around sudden sounds, convinced that his world was no longer basically safe.

That same self-judgment also shaped what he did to get through the day. Ravi began arranging himself against walls in conference rooms, waiting areas, and even at staff lunches so that no one could come up behind him. When the sense of danger was this constant, these precautions felt to Ravi less like choices than like the only way to get through the day; staying near exits, avoiding empty rooms, and sometimes hurting himself to break the surge of alarm were all attempts to make the threat feel briefly more manageable. At the nonprofit office, if a meeting room filled before he could choose the chair he wanted, he would hover near the door or find a reason not to stay. He increasingly avoided being alone in a room or a building, especially near closing time, because being alone with his own reactions felt intolerable and, to him, further proof that he could not manage what had happened. On his worst evenings, overwhelmed and disgusted with himself for still being so affected, he hurt himself physically to release the pressure, a private act he described less as wanting to die than as needing a sharp sensation that cut through the emotional flooding.

The memories themselves tightened this pattern. When the assault returned, it did not feel like a distant recollection. He heard the sounds in his head and felt pain in his body, and those episodes left him desperate not to be by himself with what might come next. After nights when he lay awake listening for any sound that might mean someone was entering his home, he would call a colleague just to keep another voice on the line. The memories also deepened his conviction that something in him had been permanently altered. Each time he could not put the experience into words, he took that as evidence not simply of distress but of damage: proof, in his mind, that he had lost access to normal feeling and normal speech.

His vigilance soon spread across his days. If someone at work touched his shoulder unexpectedly, Ravi startled violently and would need several minutes to recover. A dropped binder, footsteps in the hallway, a door opening without warning could pull him instantly into scanning mode. That constant readiness for threat wore him down and fed his bleak conclusions about himself. He began to think, if he were not so weak, he would not have to live like this; if he were not fundamentally altered, he would not be measuring every room for exits and walls. At the same time, the very strategies he relied on kept the danger feeling immediate. Sitting with his back to the wall made him scrutinize every movement in the room. Avoiding being alone meant he never learned that solitude could pass without catastrophe. Hurting himself brought momentary release, but afterward he felt even more ashamed and more certain that he was beyond ordinary help.

By the time he sought treatment, the pattern had become his life. He was staying late at the nonprofit less often because the empty office felt unbearable, and coworkers had noticed how rigid he became in meetings if someone stood behind him. He came in after a recent evening when a noise in his apartment hallway triggered the sounds of the assault so vividly that he ended up injuring himself and then sitting awake until dawn, convinced he was losing whatever remained of his old self. What frightened him most was that this was now permanent—that he would always be outside other people, always listening, always braced. What he hoped, though he said it carefully, was not to erase what happened but to be able to be alone in a room again without feeling hunted by it.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explicitly show Ravi’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the traumatic memory within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly show Ravi’s sense of threat leading to or producing negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
